screens.title: How many steps?
screens.text: This AVL tree holds 16 keys. What is the maximum number of comparisons a search could require?
screens.reveal: A search needs at most 5 comparisons. The tree has height 4, so it has 5 levels, and a search makes at most one comparison on each level, even though the tree holds 16 keys.

screens.title: Goal
screens.text: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to trace a search in an AVL tree and explain why it needs only O(log n) comparisons.

task.stem: In the BST lectures, how did a search decide where to go next?
task.hint: This question checks whether you can follow a search path. Compare the key with the node, and then go left or right.

options.text: It visited the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree.
options.explanation: That is an in-order traversal, which visits every node. A search follows one path.

options.text: It went to the child with the smaller balance factor.
options.explanation: A search never looks at balance factors. It compares keys only.

options.text: It compared the key with the node. It stopped if they were equal, went left if the key was smaller and went right if it was larger.
options.explanation: AVL search is exactly this BST search.

screens.title: Search, step by step
screens.text: Watch the search for 30. The matching line of the pseudocode lights up at each step.
screens.caption: Compare the key with the node. If the key is smaller, go left. If it is larger, go right.
steps: 30 is larger than 20, so the search goes right.
30 is smaller than 40, so the search goes left.
30 equals 30, so the key is found.

screens.title: When the key is not there
screens.caption: When the next branch is empty, the key is not in the tree, so the search returns null.
steps: 35 is larger than 20, so the search goes right.
35 is smaller than 40, so the search goes left.
35 is larger than 30, so the search goes right.
The right branch of 30 is empty, so 35 is not in the tree.

screens.title: Loop and recursive versions
screens.text: The loop version is the natural fit. A search follows a single path from the root, so there is nothing to come back to. The recursive version does the same work. Each call handles one node and calls itself on one branch only, as its last action. This is called tail recursion.

screens.title: Why search is O(log n)
points: A search makes at most one comparison per level, so it needs at most height + 1 comparisons.
Each comparison rules out one branch and everything in it. This is decrease and conquer, the same idea as binary search on a sorted array.
The AVL rule keeps the height at most roughly 1.44 log(n + 2) − 1.328.
With 1,000,000 keys, the height is at most 27, so a search needs at most 28 comparisons. A plain BST with the same keys could need 1,000,000.
screens.showRule: A search needs at most height + 1 comparisons, and the height of an AVL tree is O(log n).

screens.title: Search ignores balance factors
screens.caption: A search reads only the keys. The balance factors are shown here, but the pseudocode never uses them. Balance matters because it limits how long the path can be.

screens.title: Be the algorithm
screens.text: Click the next node that the search visits. The matching line of the pseudocode lights up, and the step counter counts the comparisons.

task.stem: Search for 9. Click the nodes in the order in which they are visited.
task.hint: This question checks whether you can follow a search path. Compare the key with the node, and then go left or right.

wrongAnswers.feedback: Check each comparison again. A smaller key goes left, and a larger key goes right.
A search follows one path from the root, and it never visits both branches of a node.

feedback.correct: 9 is larger than 7, so the search goes right. 9 is smaller than 13, so it goes left. 9 is smaller than 11, so it goes left. 9 equals 9, so the key is found after 4 comparisons.
feedback.incorrect: 9 is larger than 7, so the search goes right. 9 is smaller than 13, so it goes left. 9 is smaller than 11, so it goes left. 9 equals 9, so the key is found after 4 comparisons.

screens.title: Be the algorithm
screens.text: The step counter never goes above 5, which is the height of this tree plus one.

task.stem: Search for 17. Click the nodes in the order in which they are visited, and then choose Not found.
task.hint: This question checks whether you can tell when a search fails. The search stops when the next branch is empty.

wrongAnswers.feedback: Check each comparison again. A smaller key goes left, and a larger key goes right.
A search follows one path from the root, and it never visits both branches of a node.

feedback.correct: 17 is larger than 7, so the search goes right. 17 is larger than 13, so it goes right. 17 is larger than 15, so it goes right. 17 is larger than 16, so it goes right. That branch is empty, so 17 is not in the tree. The search made 4 comparisons.

screens.title: Lesson check
screens.text: This check has one question for each assessment criterion of the lesson's objective. You can re-attempt each question once, and the Hint button is always available.

screens.title: Summary
points: AVL search is the same as BST search. Compare the key with the node, and then go left or right.
The search stops at the key if it is found, or at an empty branch if it is not.
A search needs at most height + 1 comparisons, and the AVL rule keeps the height O(log n).
